# Introduction and Motivation

The acquisition of productive vocabulary during early childhood is one of the most intensively studied phenomena in developmental psycholinguistics. The period between **16 and 30 months of age** represents a critical window of rapid lexical development, characterised by what researchers have long described as a *vocabulary explosion* — a phase of accelerated growth in which children transition from producing a handful of words to several hundred (Bloom, 1993; Fenson et al., 1994). Understanding the trajectory of this growth, quantifying its enormous individual variability, and identifying the demographic and environmental factors that modulate its pace has both fundamental scientific importance and direct clinical relevance: vocabulary size at 24 months is among the strongest early predictors of later language abilities, academic achievement, and cognitive development (Marchman & Fernald, 2008; Hart & Risley, 1995).

## The Statistical Challenge

From a statistical modelling perspective, productive vocabulary scores present several challenges that make standard approaches inadequate. First, vocabulary counts are **discrete, non-negative, and bounded above** by the instrument ceiling (680 words on the CDI WS form), ruling out the Normal distribution as a strictly correct likelihood. Second, the empirical variance-to-mean ratio in the data ranges from 55 to 122 across monthly age groups — far exceeding the value of 1 required by the Poisson distribution — indicating massive **overdispersion** that cannot be accommodated without an additional dispersion parameter. Third, the distribution of vocabulary scores **changes shape systematically with age**: strongly right-skewed at 16 months (most children near zero), approximately symmetric at 22–23 months, and left-skewed at 28–30 months as children approach the CDI ceiling. Fourth, the **individual variability is enormous**: at 24 months, children of the same age may produce anywhere from fewer than 10 to over 600 words (Frank et al., 2017), a heterogeneity that a population-level model cannot represent.

These features collectively motivate a **Bayesian hierarchical Negative Binomial model**. The Negative Binomial distribution naturally accommodates overdispersed count data through an additional dispersion parameter $r$; the hierarchical structure enables partial pooling of information across age groups; and the Bayesian framework provides full posterior uncertainty quantification, principled prior incorporation, and a formal model comparison criterion (DIC) that balances fit against complexity.

## Covariates and Literature Background

Beyond the age trajectory, the developmental literature identifies several individual-level factors that systematically modulate vocabulary growth. **Sex** is the most consistently documented: girls are reported to have larger productive vocabularies than boys at comparable ages throughout the second year of life (Fenson et al., 1994; Eriksson et al., 2012), a difference that has been attributed to earlier maturation of left-hemisphere language areas (Huttenlocher et al., 1991) and greater sensitivity to linguistic input (Bates et al., 1994). The sex difference may operate on the *level* of the vocabulary plateau (asymptotic effect) or on the *rate* of acquisition (growth rate effect) — a distinction that our modelling framework explicitly tests.

**Caregiver education** is a proxy for the quantity and quality of linguistic input: Hart & Risley (1995) documented that children from higher-SES families hear approximately 30 million more words by age 3 than children from lower-SES families, producing substantial differences in vocabulary growth rates. Crucially, their analysis suggests this operates primarily on the *rate* of acquisition rather than the eventual ceiling — again a distinction that our model can test directly.

**Birth order** has also been documented as a relevant factor: first-born children tend to receive more individual linguistic input from caregivers than later-born children, resulting in richer early vocabularies (Hoff, 2003). The 43% rate of missing data for this variable in our dataset motivates its treatment through **Bayesian missing data imputation** — a natural capability of JAGS that allows the posterior to integrate over the uncertainty in unobserved birth-order values.

Finally, the possibility of an **age × sex interaction** — with sex differences diverging progressively during the vocabulary explosion — has been documented by Bornstein et al. (2004), and is tested through a hierarchical model in which the sex effect is allowed to vary across monthly age groups.

## Structure of the Analysis

This document presents a fully Bayesian analysis of early vocabulary growth structured as follows: Section 2 describes the WordBank dataset and the Marchman subsample used for modelling. Section 3 presents the exploratory data analysis that motivates the model choices. Section 4 introduces the Negative Binomial likelihood and presents six models of increasing complexity. Section 5 reports the parameter recovery study. Section 6 presents MCMC convergence diagnostics. Sections 7 and 8 present the formal model checking (Bayesian p-value) and the frequentist comparison (bonus analyses). Section 9 discusses the results and their implications.

# Dataset Description

## The WordBank Database

Data come from the **WordBank database** (wordbank.stanford.edu), an open-access repository aggregating MacArthur-Bates CDI data from multiple research groups worldwide (Frank et al., 2017). WordBank currently contains CDI data from over 80,000 children across more than 20 languages. We use the **CDI Words and Sentences form (WS)**, designed for children aged 16–30 months, which contains a checklist of **680 common English words**. The *productive vocabulary* score — the number of words a child produces according to parent report — ranges from 0 to 680 and serves as the response variable throughout.

```{r load-data}
# ── Robust data loading: tries .rds cache first, then WordBank API ─────────
# To create the cache from a working session: saveRDS(data_full, "data_full.rds")

rds_path <- "data_full.rds"

if (file.exists(rds_path)) {

  data_full <- readRDS(rds_path)
  cat("Loaded from cache:", nrow(data_full), "observations\n")

} else {

  message("data_full.rds not found — attempting WordBank API...")
  Sys.setenv(WORDBANK_URL = "https://wordbank.stanford.edu")

  tryCatch({
    data_full <- get_administration_data(
      language = "English (American)", form = "WS",
      include_demographic_info = TRUE
    )
  }, error = function(e) {
    data_full <<- NULL
  })

  if (is.null(data_full) || nrow(data_full) == 0) {
    stop(paste(
      "Could not load data_full.",
      "WordBank is unreachable and no local cache found.",
      "Please run this in an R console when WordBank is available:",
      "  data_full <- get_administration_data(",
      "    language = 'English (American)', form = 'WS',",
      "    include_demographic_info = TRUE)",
      "  saveRDS(data_full, 'data_full.rds')",
      sep = "\n"
    ))
  }

  saveRDS(data_full, rds_path)
  cat("Downloaded and cached:", nrow(data_full), "observations\n")
}

cat("Variables:", paste(names(data_full), collapse=", "), "\n")
```

## Dataset Heterogeneity and the Marchman Subsample

The full dataset aggregates contributions from 9 independent research groups. Before modelling, we investigate whether these datasets are homogeneous.

```{r dataset-heterogeneity}
data_full %>%
  filter(age >= 16, age <= 30) %>%
  count(dataset_name, sort=TRUE)
```

```{r dataset-bias}
# Mean productive vocabulary by dataset at ages 28-30
data_full %>%
  filter(age >= 28, age <= 30) %>%
  group_by(age, dataset_name) %>%
  summarise(n=n(), mean_prod=round(mean(production),1), .groups="drop") %>%
  arrange(age, desc(mean_prod))
```

The cross-tabulation reveals substantial heterogeneity: at age 30, the **Hoff dataset** shows a mean of 288 words versus Marchman's 487 — a difference of nearly 200 words. This reflects genuine sampling differences: Hoff recruited families across SES strata (Hoff, 2003), while Poulin-Dubois focused on bilingual children (Pearson et al., 1993), both known to produce lower CDI scores on average. The **Marchman dataset** (Marchman & Fernald, 2008) is the largest single contributor (n = 5,039), covers all 15 monthly age groups from 16 to 30 months, and provides a homogeneous monolingual English-learning sample with well-documented collection conditions. We restrict all analyses to this dataset.

```{r marchman-filter}
df_march <- data_full %>%
  filter(dataset_name == "Marchman", age >= 16, age <= 30,
         !is.na(production)) %>%
  select(age, production, sex, birth_order, caregiver_education)

dim(df_march)
colSums(is.na(df_march))
```

## Covariates Available

```{r covariate-summary}
cat("Sex distribution:\n")
table(df_march$sex, useNA="always")

cat("\nBirth order (condensed):\n")
table(df_march$birth_order, useNA="always")

cat("\nCaregiver education:\n")
table(df_march$caregiver_education, useNA="always")

# Mean vocabulary by sex
df_march %>%
  filter(!is.na(sex)) %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(n=n(), mean_prod=round(mean(production),1), sd_prod=round(sd(production),1))
```

Sex is complete (0 NA), education has only 8 NA, and birth order has 2,180 NA (43%). The sex difference of 37 words (288 female vs. 251 male) is immediately apparent and consistent with Fenson et al. (1994).
