# Posterior Predictive Distributions and Clinical Interpretation

## From Inference to Prediction

Statistical inference tells us *what the model has learned* from data — the posterior distributions of $\alpha_j$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, and $r$. But the scientifically and clinically most useful output is the **posterior predictive distribution**: the full probability distribution over vocabulary scores for a new child of given age and sex, integrating over all parameter uncertainty.

For a new child $\tilde{y}$ of age $\tilde{x}$ and sex $s$, the posterior predictive distribution is:

$$p(\tilde{y} \mid y_{\text{obs}}) = \int p(\tilde{y} \mid \theta) \cdot p(\theta \mid y_{\text{obs}}) \, d\theta$$

In practice, this is approximated by drawing $\theta^{(s)}$ from the MCMC posterior, computing $\mu^{(s)} = (\alpha_{j}^{(s)} + \gamma^{(s)} \cdot s) \cdot (1 - e^{-\beta^{(s)}(\tilde{x}-8)})$, and then drawing $\tilde{y}^{(s)} \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu^{(s)}, r^{(s)})$. The resulting sample $\{\tilde{y}^{(s)}\}$ represents the full predictive uncertainty, incorporating both **parameter uncertainty** (epistemic) and **intrinsic child-to-child variability** (aleatoric).

This is a key strength of the Bayesian framework: frequentist point estimates give a single predicted value with a confidence interval that technically refers to repeated sampling of datasets, not to individual children. The posterior predictive distribution directly answers the clinician's question: *"Given what I know about this child's age and sex, what is the probability that their vocabulary falls below a given threshold?"*

## Posterior Predictive Distributions by Age and Sex

```{r predictive-plot, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Posterior predictive distributions for productive vocabulary at ages 18, 24, and 30 months, by sex (NB3 model). Blue = male, red = female. The vertical dotted line marks the CDI ceiling of 680 words. At 18 months the distributions are nearly identical and strongly right-skewed; by 24 months maximum inter-individual divergence is reached; at 30 months the left shift reflects ceiling compression. The female advantage (52 words on the asymptote) is visible but modest relative to the enormous within-sex variability."}
post3 <- fit_nb3$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
ages_pred <- c(18, 24, 30)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (eta in ages_pred) {
  j     <- eta - 15
  a_idx <- paste0("alpha[", j, "]")
  n_pred <- 5000
  idx_s  <- sample(nrow(post3), n_pred, replace = TRUE)

  mu_male   <- post3[idx_s, a_idx] *
               (1 - exp(-post3[idx_s, "beta"] * (eta - 8)))
  mu_female <- (post3[idx_s, a_idx] + post3[idx_s, "gamma"]) *
               (1 - exp(-post3[idx_s, "beta"] * (eta - 8)))

  y_pred_male   <- pmin(rnbinom(n_pred, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_male),   680)
  y_pred_female <- pmin(rnbinom(n_pred, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_female), 680)

  d_m <- density(y_pred_male,   from=0, to=700)
  d_f <- density(y_pred_female, from=0, to=700)

  plot(d_m, col=col_blue, lwd=2.5,
       xlim=c(0, 720), ylim=c(0, max(d_m$y, d_f$y)*1.15),
       main=paste0("Age: ", eta, " months"),
       xlab="Productive vocabulary", ylab="Density")
  polygon(d_m, col=adjustcolor(col_blue, 0.12), border=NA)
  lines(d_f, col=col_red, lwd=2.5)
  polygon(d_f, col=adjustcolor(col_red, 0.12), border=NA)
  abline(v=680, col="gray50", lty=3, lwd=1.5)

  legend("topright", bty="n",
         legend=c(sprintf("Male:   median=%d", round(median(y_pred_male))),
                  sprintf("Female: median=%d", round(median(y_pred_female)))),
         col=c(col_blue, col_red), lwd=2, cex=0.82)
}
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

While the three-panel predictive comparison above shows three age "snapshots", it is also useful to see the predictive percentiles evolve *continuously* across the full 16–30 month range — a so-called fan chart, commonly used in forecasting to communicate widening uncertainty over a horizon. Here the "horizon" is age rather than calendar time, but the visual logic is identical: it shows at a glance both the central predicted trajectory and how rapidly the plausible range of outcomes expands as children move through the vocabulary explosion.

```{r predictive-fanchart, fig.cap="Posterior predictive 'fan chart' for productive vocabulary across the full 16–30 month age range, separately for boys (left) and girls (right), based on the NB3 model. Shaded bands show the 10th–90th (light) and 25th–75th (dark) posterior predictive percentile ranges; the solid line is the predictive median. Both fans widen rapidly between 18 and 24 months — the vocabulary explosion window — and are visibly clipped at the 680-word ceiling for the oldest ages, especially for girls, whose higher central tendency makes ceiling contact more likely."}
ages_fan <- 16:30
fan_male <- fan_female <- matrix(NA, nrow=length(ages_fan), ncol=5)
colnames(fan_male) <- colnames(fan_female) <- c("p10","p25","p50","p75","p90")

set.seed(7)
for (k in seq_along(ages_fan)) {
  eta <- ages_fan[k]; j <- eta-15; a_idx <- paste0("alpha[",j,"]")
  idx_s <- sample(nrow(post3), 4000, replace=TRUE)
  mu_m <- post3[idx_s,a_idx]*(1-exp(-post3[idx_s,"beta"]*(eta-8)))
  mu_f <- (post3[idx_s,a_idx]+post3[idx_s,"gamma"])*(1-exp(-post3[idx_s,"beta"]*(eta-8)))
  ym <- pmin(rnbinom(4000, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_m), 680)
  yf <- pmin(rnbinom(4000, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_f), 680)
  fan_male[k,]   <- quantile(ym, c(.10,.25,.50,.75,.90))
  fan_female[k,] <- quantile(yf, c(.10,.25,.50,.75,.90))
}

par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4,4,3,1))
plot(ages_fan, fan_male[,"p50"], type="n", ylim=c(0,690),
     xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Productive vocabulary", main="Boys - predictive fan")
polygon(c(ages_fan,rev(ages_fan)), c(fan_male[,"p10"],rev(fan_male[,"p90"])),
        col=adjustcolor(col_blue,0.18), border=NA)
polygon(c(ages_fan,rev(ages_fan)), c(fan_male[,"p25"],rev(fan_male[,"p75"])),
        col=adjustcolor(col_blue,0.35), border=NA)
lines(ages_fan, fan_male[,"p50"], col=col_blue, lwd=2.5)
abline(h=680, col=col_red, lty=3)

plot(ages_fan, fan_female[,"p50"], type="n", ylim=c(0,690),
     xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Productive vocabulary", main="Girls - predictive fan")
polygon(c(ages_fan,rev(ages_fan)), c(fan_female[,"p10"],rev(fan_female[,"p90"])),
        col=adjustcolor(col_red,0.18), border=NA)
polygon(c(ages_fan,rev(ages_fan)), c(fan_female[,"p25"],rev(fan_female[,"p75"])),
        col=adjustcolor(col_red,0.35), border=NA)
lines(ages_fan, fan_female[,"p50"], col=col_red, lwd=2.5)
abline(h=680, col=col_red, lty=3)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

Two features stand out in the fan chart above that were less visible in the three-snapshot comparison. First, the **rate of fan widening is itself age-dependent**: the bands are relatively narrow and close together at 16–18 months, expand rapidly through 20–24 months, and then begin to compress again as the upper bound presses against the 680-word ceiling — a direct visual signature of the changing skewness documented in the EDA. Second, **ceiling clipping is visibly asymmetric between the sexes**: because girls have a higher central tendency at every age, their 90th percentile band touches the 680 ceiling roughly two months earlier than boys' (around 24–25 months for girls vs. 26–27 months for boys), even though the underlying NegBin model treats both sexes with the same dispersion parameter $r$. This is a subtle but important consequence of the asymptotic growth model interacting with a bounded instrument, and is the most direct illustration of why the CDI ceiling, discussed as a limitation in Section 9.2, is not merely a theoretical concern but visibly distorts the right tail of the predictive distribution for precisely the children — and the sex — for whom the model predicts the most precocious vocabulary development.

## Predictive Reference Table

The table below constitutes the main **predictive output** of the analysis: for each age and sex, it reports the posterior predictive median (50th percentile) and the 10th--90th percentile band. Values are truncated at 680 (CDI ceiling) via `pmin(..., 680)`.

```{r predictive-table}
set.seed(42)
pred_rows <- list()

for (eta in c(18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30)) {
  j     <- eta - 15
  a_idx <- paste0("alpha[", j, "]")
  idx_s <- sample(nrow(post3), 5000, replace = TRUE)

  mu_m <- post3[idx_s, a_idx] *
          (1 - exp(-post3[idx_s,"beta"] * (eta-8)))
  mu_f <- (post3[idx_s, a_idx] + post3[idx_s,"gamma"]) *
          (1 - exp(-post3[idx_s,"beta"] * (eta-8)))

  ypm <- pmin(rnbinom(5000, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_m), 680)
  ypf <- pmin(rnbinom(5000, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_f), 680)

  pred_rows[[length(pred_rows)+1]] <- data.frame(
    Age_months    = eta,
    Male_p10      = round(quantile(ypm, 0.10)),
    Male_p50      = round(median(ypm)),
    Male_p90      = round(quantile(ypm, 0.90)),
    Female_p10    = round(quantile(ypf, 0.10)),
    Female_p50    = round(median(ypf)),
    Female_p90    = round(quantile(ypf, 0.90)),
    Sex_gap_median= round(median(ypf) - median(ypm))
  )
}

pred_table <- do.call(rbind, pred_rows)
print(pred_table, row.names=FALSE)
```

## Interpretation

**Three developmental phases** emerge clearly from the predictive distributions:

**Phase 1 — Pre-explosion (18--20 months).** Both distributions are strongly right-skewed, with the majority of children producing fewer than 100 words and a long tail extending toward 200--250. The sex gap at the median is modest (approximately 17--20 words), while the 10th--90th percentile band already spans over 200 words, confirming that inter-individual variability dominates any group-level difference at this age. This is consistent with Bloom's (1993) observation that the timing of vocabulary onset is the primary source of variability in early language development.

**Phase 2 — Explosion (22--24 months).** This is the period of maximum divergence: the 10th--90th band reaches over 500 words (59--565 for males at 24 months). The shape transitions from right-skewed to approximately uniform, reflecting the simultaneous presence of children who have not yet begun rapid vocabulary growth and children who are already near the CDI ceiling. The female advantage reaches approximately 24 words at the median (247 vs 223), still modest relative to the total spread.

**Phase 3 — Ceiling approach (26--30 months).** The 90th percentile is constrained at 680 for both sexes from age 26 onward (after `pmin` truncation), reflecting the CDI ceiling effect. The median continues to rise (305 male, 335 female at 26 months; 385 male, 398 female at 30 months), but the upper tail is artificially compressed. This is the clearest manifestation of the CDI ceiling limitation: a child who produces all 680 listed words may in fact have a much larger active vocabulary, but the instrument cannot detect this.

**The sex gap is real but clinically modest.** The posterior predictive median difference between females and males ranges from 17 words (18 months) to 30 words (26 months) — a consistent advantage that is statistically credible (CI on $\gamma$ excludes zero) but small relative to the enormous within-sex variability. A clinician using these distributions for developmental screening would find that the 10th--90th percentile bands of males and females overlap almost completely at every age. The tables above are therefore best interpreted as **sex-stratified normative references** rather than as evidence of a clinically actionable sex difference.

<div class="finding">
**Predictive conclusion.** The Bayesian hierarchical NegBin model (NB3) yields sex-stratified posterior predictive distributions that can serve as normative references for vocabulary screening. At 24 months — the most clinically relevant milestone — the model predicts a male median of 223 words (10th--90th percentile: 59--565) and a female median of 247 words (64--624). The enormous width of these bands reflects genuine inter-individual variability, not model uncertainty: even a "perfect" model of average trajectories would face this irreducible aleatoric uncertainty, captured by the NegBin dispersion parameter $\hat{r} \approx 1.65$.
</div>

# Discussion and Conclusions

## A Visual Executive Summary

Before discussing each finding in prose, it is useful to assemble the project's central numerical results into a single visual summary, bringing together the four pieces of evidence that jointly justify the modelling choices made throughout this report: the overdispersion that rules out Poisson, the DIC evidence that ranks the six models, the sex effect that is real but modest, and the irreducible width of the predictive distribution.

```{r executive-summary-plot, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Executive summary of the four central findings. Top-left: overdispersion ratio by age (all points far above the Poisson threshold of 1). Top-right: DIC by model, with NB2 as reference. Bottom-left: estimated sex gap on alpha (NB3) and on beta (NB6, converted to an implied gap in months-to-half-asymptote), both with 95% credible intervals. Bottom-right: predictive median and 80% band at 24 months, the clinically pivotal vocabulary-explosion mid-point, for boys vs girls."}
par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar=c(4,4,3,1))

# Panel 1: overdispersion ratio by age
plot(desc$age, desc$var_mean_ratio, type="b", pch=16, col=col_red, lwd=2,
     xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Var / Mean", main="(A) Overdispersion by age",
     ylim=c(0,160))
abline(h=1, col="gray50", lty=2, lwd=1.5)
text(17, 10, "Poisson threshold = 1", cex=0.7, col="gray40", pos=3)

# Panel 2: DIC by model (NegBin models only for readability — P0 would dwarf the others)
nb_dic_vals  <- dic_vals[2:7]
nb_dic_names <- dic_table$Model[2:7]
nb_dic_cols  <- c(col_red, col_green, col_green, col_green, "#CC8800", "#CC8800")
barplot(pmin(nb_dic_vals, 6440), col=adjustcolor(nb_dic_cols, 0.75), border=nb_dic_cols,
        ylim=c(6390, 6440), xpd=FALSE, ylab="DIC", main="(B) DIC by NegBin model",
        names.arg=nb_dic_names, cex.names=0.7)
abline(h=dic_table$DIC[3], col=col_green, lty=2)  # NB2 is row 3 (after P0)

# Panel 3: sex gap comparison
gap_alpha   <- mean(post3_cmp[,"gamma"])
gap_alpha_ci<- quantile(post3_cmp[,"gamma"], c(.025,.975))
half_male   <- log(2)/post6_cmp[,"beta[1]"]
half_female <- log(2)/post6_cmp[,"beta[2]"]
gap_months  <- mean(half_male - half_female)
gap_months_ci <- quantile(half_male - half_female, c(.025,.975))

bp2 <- barplot(c(gap_alpha, NA), ylim=c(0,120), col=col_green,
               names.arg=c("Sex gap on\nvocabulary level\n(words, NB3)",""),
               main="(C) Sex effects: level vs timing", ylab="Effect size")
arrows(bp2[1], gap_alpha_ci[1], bp2[1], gap_alpha_ci[2], angle=90, code=3, length=0.05)
par(new=TRUE)
bp3 <- barplot(c(NA, gap_months), ylim=c(0,6), col=col_purp, axes=FALSE,
               names.arg=c("","Sex gap on\ntiming\n(months, NB6)"), ylab="")
axis(4)
mtext("Months earlier (girls)", side=4, line=2.2, cex=0.7)
arrows(bp3[2], gap_months_ci[1], bp3[2], gap_months_ci[2], angle=90, code=3, length=0.05)

# Panel 4: predictive band at 24 months
j24 <- 24-15; a_idx24 <- paste0("alpha[",j24,"]")
idx24 <- sample(nrow(post3), 4000, replace=TRUE)
mu_m24 <- post3[idx24,a_idx24]*(1-exp(-post3[idx24,"beta"]*(24-8)))
mu_f24 <- (post3[idx24,a_idx24]+post3[idx24,"gamma"])*(1-exp(-post3[idx24,"beta"]*(24-8)))
ym24 <- pmin(rnbinom(4000,size=post3[idx24,"r"],mu=mu_m24),680)
yf24 <- pmin(rnbinom(4000,size=post3[idx24,"r"],mu=mu_f24),680)

boxplot(list(Boys=ym24, Girls=yf24), col=c(adjustcolor(col_blue,0.5),adjustcolor(col_red,0.5)),
        main="(D) Predictive distribution at 24mo", ylab="Productive vocabulary")

par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

Panel (A) shows that overdispersion is not an artefact of any single age group but a pervasive feature present from 16 to 30 months. Panel (B) shows the dominance of the hierarchical structure (NB2) over the population baseline (NB1), with the covariate models clustering in a narrow band around NB2. Panel (C) directly contrasts the two ways the sex effect was tested: as a roughly 52-word gap on the vocabulary ceiling (NB3) and as a roughly 3–4 month head-start in reaching the half-asymptote (NB6) — both credible intervals exclude zero, visually confirming Findings 2 and 3 discussed below. Panel (D) returns to the predictive question that motivates the entire exercise: at the clinically pivotal 24-month mark, boys' and girls' predictive distributions overlap substantially despite the statistically credible group-level difference, encapsulating the central tension of this analysis between statistical significance and individual-level predictive utility.

## Summary of Findings

This project has presented a fully Bayesian analysis of early vocabulary growth in children aged 16–30 months, using data from the WordBank database (Frank et al., 2017). Following the suggestion to use discrete count likelihoods for CDI data, all models employ the Negative Binomial distribution, motivated by the extreme overdispersion documented in the data (variance/mean ratios of 55–154 across age groups). Six models of increasing complexity were fitted and compared via DIC, with formal convergence diagnostics, a Bayesian p-value model check, and a frequentist comparison.

**Finding 1: The Negative Binomial likelihood is essential — and the Poisson is catastrophically inadequate.** The estimated dispersion $\hat{r} \approx 1.4$–1.6 confirms massive overdispersion relative to Poisson across all NegBin models. More concretely, the Poisson model P0 — fitted with the identical mean function as NB1 but without the latent Gamma layer — achieves a DIC hundreds of points higher than every NegBin model. This gap is a pure measure of the cost of the Poisson constraint $\text{Var}(y_i) = \mu_i$: with observed variance/mean ratios of 55–154, the Poisson assigns negligible probability to the actual spread of vocabulary scores. The NegBin resolves this through its Poisson-Gamma mixture structure: every child $i$ has a latent individual rate $\lambda_i \sim \text{Gamma}(r, r/\mu_i)$ capturing unmeasured between-child heterogeneity, and marginally $y_i \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu_i, r)$.

**Finding 2: Hierarchical structure is the dominant modelling choice.** The transition from population-level NB1 to hierarchical NB2 yields $\Delta$DIC = 87.3 — by far the largest single improvement in the analysis. Age-specific asymptotes $\alpha_j$ correctly capture the structured heterogeneity in growth trajectories, resolving the biological implausibility of NB1's single shared asymptote and enabling biologically meaningful estimates ($\hat{\mu}_\alpha \approx 424$ words, $\hat{\beta} \approx 0.059$).

**Finding 3: Sex has a real but modest predictive contribution.** Both NB3 (sex on level, $\hat{\gamma} = 52$ words, CI excludes zero) and NB6 (sex on rate, $\hat{\delta}_\beta = 0.016$, CI excludes zero) confirm the literature prediction of a female advantage (Fenson et al., 1994; Bates et al., 1994). NB6 provides the richer biological interpretation: girls not only have higher vocabulary ceilings but approach them approximately 4 months earlier than boys — a finding consistent with earlier left-hemisphere language maturation (Huttenlocher et al., 1991). However, both models improve DIC by only 3–5 points, below the threshold for strong evidence, reflecting the high within-age variability that dominates individual differences.

**Finding 4: Education and the age×sex interaction are not supported in this sample.** The null result for caregiver education (NB_edu, DIC worse than NB2) is likely attributable to the relative SES homogeneity of the Marchman sample — the Hart & Risley (1995) effect requires a sample with genuine SES variation to detect. The age×sex interaction (NB_int) is biologically plausible (Bornstein et al., 2004) but statistically underpowered given approximately 33 children per monthly age group.

**Finding 5: Bayesian model checking confirms adequate calibration.** The Bayesian p-value of $p_B = 0.564$ for NB2 confirms that the model is well-calibrated with respect to the chi-square discrepancy. The hierarchical structure and Bayesian shrinkage provide substantially more stable estimates than per-group MLE for data-poor age groups — the comparison in Section 8 confirms differences of 100–155 words at ages 16–22 months, converging as predicted by the Bernstein-von Mises theorem at data-rich older ages.

## Limitations

- **Cross-sectional data**: Each child is observed once, preventing estimation of individual growth trajectories. A longitudinal design would enable true random-effects growth curve modelling (Pinheiro & Bates, 2000).

- **CDI ceiling**: The NegBin likelihood does not explicitly model the hard upper bound of 680 words. A Tobit or censored regression framework would handle this more formally.

- **Sample homogeneity**: The Marchman dataset provides good internal validity but limited SES and ethnic diversity, reducing generalisability and statistical power to detect education and birth-order effects. A multi-dataset analysis with dataset-level random effects (tested exploratorily, $\Delta$DIC = 132.7) would recover both power and generalisability.

- **Birth order**: The 43% missing rate for birth_order prevented its inclusion as a formal covariate despite documented effects (Hoff, 2003). Bayesian multiple imputation within JAGS is technically feasible but was not pursued here.

## Future Directions

- **Multi-dataset hierarchical model** with a dataset-level random effect, enabling full use of all 9,093 WordBank observations while accounting for sampling heterogeneity
- **Longitudinal data** for individual growth curve estimation
- **Censored NegBin** or Beta-Binomial to address the CDI ceiling more formally
- **Birth order with Bayesian imputation** to recover this clinically relevant predictor

# Helper: save a base-R plot
save_fig <- function(filename, expr, w=9, h=5) {
  pdf(file.path("latex_figures", paste0(filename, ".pdf")), width=w, height=h)
  force(expr)
  invisible(dev.off())
  cat("Saved:", filename, "\n")
}

# Helper: save a ggplot
save_gg <- function(filename, p, w=9, h=5) {
  ggplot2::ggsave(
    file.path("latex_figures", paste0(filename, ".pdf")),
    plot=p, width=w, height=h)
  cat("Saved:", filename, "\n")
}

# ── fig01_growth_trajectory (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig01_growth_trajectory", {
  par(mfrow=c(1,2))
  
  # Percentile plot

    group_by(age) %>%
    summarise(p10=quantile(production,.10), p50=quantile(production,.50),
              p90=quantile(production,.90), .groups="drop")
  
  plot(pct_data$age, pct_data$p50, type="l", col=col_red, lwd=2.5,
       ylim=c(0,680), xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Words produced",
       main="Growth trajectory (Marchman, n=5,039)")
  polygon(c(pct_data$age, rev(pct_data$age)),
          c(pct_data$p10, rev(pct_data$p90)),
          col=adjustcolor(col_teal,.4), border=NA)
  lines(pct_data$age, pct_data$p10, col=col_blue, lty=2)
  lines(pct_data$age, pct_data$p90, col=col_blue, lty=2)

  # Sex plot

# ── fig02_overdispersion_bars (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig02_overdispersion_bars", {
  mv_data <- df_march %>%
    group_by(age) %>%
    summarise(mean_v = mean(production), var_v = var(production), .groups="drop") %>%
    mutate(ratio = round(var_v / mean_v, 0))
  
  r_ref <- 1.6
  negbin_var <- mv_data$mean_v + mv_data$mean_v^2 / r_ref
  
  bar_matrix <- rbind(Observed = mv_data$var_v,
                       Poisson  = mv_data$mean_v,
                       NegBin   = negbin_var)
  colnames(bar_matrix) <- mv_data$age
  
  # Reserve a dedicated strip at the top of the figure for the legend,
  # so it never overlaps the bars regardless of their height
  layout(matrix(c(1,2), nrow=2), heights=c(1, 5))
  
  par(mar=c(0,4,0,1))
  plot.new()
  legend("center", horiz=TRUE, bty="n", cex=0.85, xpd=NA, x.intersp=0.6, text.width=NA,
         legend=c("Observed", "Poisson", "NegBin (r=1.6)", "Ratio (obs/Poisson)"),
         fill=c(col_red, "gray70", col_purp, NA), border=NA,
         text.col=c("black","black","black",col_purp))
  
  par(mar=c(5,4,2,1))
  bp <- barplot(bar_matrix, beside=TRUE, col=c(col_red, "gray70", col_purp),
                border=NA, log="y", ylim=c(1, max(mv_data$var_v)*2.2),
                xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Variance (log scale)")
  
  ratio_x <- bp[1,] + (bp[2,]-bp[1,])
  text(ratio_x, mv_data$var_v, labels=paste0(mv_data$ratio,"x"),
       pos=3, cex=0.8, col=col_purp, font=2, xpd=NA)
  
  layout(1)  # reset layout for subsequent plots
}, w=9, h=6)

# ── fig06_p0_vs_nb1 (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig06_p0_vs_nb1", {
  age_grid_p <- 16:30
  n_draw_p   <- 2000
  post_p0    <- fit_p0$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  post_nb1   <- fit_nb1$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  
  par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4,4,3,1))
  
  for (mod in c("Poisson","NegBin")) {
    pm    <- if(mod=="Poisson") post_p0 else post_nb1
    set.seed(5)
    idx_p <- sample(nrow(pm), n_draw_p, replace=TRUE)
    pred_mu <- sapply(age_grid_p, function(a)
      pm[idx_p,"alpha"] * (1-exp(-pm[idx_p,"beta"]*(a-8))))
    if (mod=="Poisson") {
      pred_lo <- sapply(1:length(age_grid_p), function(k)
        quantile(qpois(0.10, pred_mu[,k]), 0.5))
      pred_hi <- sapply(1:length(age_grid_p), function(k)
        quantile(qpois(0.90, pred_mu[,k]), 0.5))
    } else {
      r_s <- pm[idx_p,"r"]
      pred_lo <- sapply(1:length(age_grid_p), function(k)
        quantile(rnbinom(n_draw_p, size=r_s, mu=pred_mu[,k]), 0.10))
      pred_hi <- sapply(1:length(age_grid_p), function(k)
        quantile(rnbinom(n_draw_p, size=r_s, mu=pred_mu[,k]), 0.90))
    }
    pred_mean <- colMeans(pred_mu)
  
    plot(jitter(df_model_cov$age, 0.6), df_model_cov$production,
         pch=16, col=adjustcolor("gray40",0.3), cex=0.6,
         xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Productive vocabulary",
         main=paste0(mod, " model — predictive band"),
         ylim=c(0,720))
    polygon(c(age_grid_p,rev(age_grid_p)), c(pred_lo,rev(pred_hi)),
            col=adjustcolor(col_blue,0.20), border=NA)
    lines(age_grid_p, pred_mean,
          col=if(mod=="Poisson") col_red else col_blue, lwd=2.5)
    abline(h=680, col="gray60", lty=3)
  }
  par(mfrow=c(1,1))
}, w=9, h=4.5)

# ── fig07_nb2_fit (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig07_nb2_fit", {
  post2_full <- fit_nb2$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  age_grid2  <- 16:30
  
  pred_mean <- pred_lo <- pred_hi <- numeric(length(age_grid2))
  set.seed(1)
  for (k in seq_along(age_grid2)) {
    eta <- age_grid2[k]
    j   <- eta - 15
    a_idx <- paste0("alpha[", j, "]")
    idx_s <- sample(nrow(post2_full), 3000, replace=TRUE)
    mu_k  <- post2_full[idx_s, a_idx] * (1 - exp(-post2_full[idx_s,"beta"]*(eta-8)))
    y_k   <- rnbinom(3000, size=post2_full[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_k)
    pred_mean[k] <- mean(mu_k)
    pred_lo[k]   <- quantile(y_k, 0.10)
    pred_hi[k]   <- quantile(y_k, 0.90)
  }
  
  plot(jitter(df_model_cov$age, 0.6), df_model_cov$production,
       pch=16, col=adjustcolor("gray40", 0.35), cex=0.7,
       xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Productive vocabulary",
       main="NB2 Fitted Curve vs Observed Data (n=500 modelling subsample)")
  polygon(c(age_grid2, rev(age_grid2)), c(pred_lo, rev(pred_hi)),
          col=adjustcolor(col_blue, 0.18), border=NA)
  lines(age_grid2, pred_mean, col=col_blue, lwd=2.8)
  abline(h=680, col=col_red, lty=3)
  legend("topleft", bty="n",
         legend=c("Observed children","Posterior mean E[y|x]","80% predictive interval"),
         col=c("gray40", col_blue, adjustcolor(col_blue,0.4)),
         pch=c(16,NA,15), lwd=c(NA,2.8,NA), pt.cex=c(0.7,NA,2.2))
}, w=9, h=5)

# ── fig08_nb3_gamma (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig08_nb3_gamma", {

          col=adjustcolor(col_purp,0.25), border=NA)

}, w=9, h=4)

# ── fig09_nb6_curves (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig09_nb6_curves", {
  post6_full <- fit_nb6$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  age_grid6  <- 16:30
  n_draw6 <- 3000
  set.seed(11)
  idx6 <- sample(nrow(post6_full), n_draw6, replace=TRUE)
  
  curve_m <- sapply(age_grid6, function(a)
    post6_full[idx6,"mu_alpha"] * (1-exp(-post6_full[idx6,"beta[1]"]*(a-8))))
  curve_f <- sapply(age_grid6, function(a)
    post6_full[idx6,"mu_alpha"] * (1-exp(-post6_full[idx6,"beta[2]"]*(a-8))))
  
  m_mean <- colMeans(curve_m); m_lo <- apply(curve_m,2,quantile,.025); m_hi <- apply(curve_m,2,quantile,.975)
  f_mean <- colMeans(curve_f); f_lo <- apply(curve_f,2,quantile,.025); f_hi <- apply(curve_f,2,quantile,.975)
  
  plot(age_grid6, m_mean, type="n", ylim=c(0,650),
       xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Predicted vocabulary",
       main="NB6: Sex-Specific Growth Rate Curves")
  polygon(c(age_grid6,rev(age_grid6)), c(m_lo,rev(m_hi)), col=adjustcolor(col_blue,0.2), border=NA)
  polygon(c(age_grid6,rev(age_grid6)), c(f_lo,rev(f_hi)), col=adjustcolor(col_red,0.2), border=NA)
  lines(age_grid6, m_mean, col=col_blue, lwd=2.5)
  lines(age_grid6, f_mean, col=col_red, lwd=2.5)
  legend("topleft", bty="n", legend=c("Boys (beta=0.049)","Girls (beta=0.065)"),
         col=c(col_blue,col_red), lwd=2.5)
}, w=9, h=4.5)

# ── fig10_edu_curves (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig10_edu_curves", {
  postE_full <- fit_edu$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  age_gridE  <- 16:30
  n_drawE <- 3000
  set.seed(13)
  idxE <- sample(nrow(postE_full), n_drawE, replace=TRUE)
  
  curve_low <- sapply(age_gridE, function(a)
    postE_full[idxE,"mu_alpha"]*(1-exp(-(postE_full[idxE,"beta"])*(a-8))))
  curve_med <- sapply(age_gridE, function(a)
    postE_full[idxE,"mu_alpha"]*(1-exp(-(postE_full[idxE,"beta"]+postE_full[idxE,"delta_edu[2]"])*(a-8))))
  curve_hi  <- sapply(age_gridE, function(a)
    postE_full[idxE,"mu_alpha"]*(1-exp(-(postE_full[idxE,"beta"]+postE_full[idxE,"delta_edu[3]"])*(a-8))))
  
  plot(age_gridE, colMeans(curve_low), type="l", lwd=2.2, col=col_blue,
       ylim=c(0,600), xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Predicted vocabulary",
       main="NB_edu: Growth Curves by Education Level (near-identical)")
  lines(age_gridE, colMeans(curve_med), lwd=2.2, col=col_green)
  lines(age_gridE, colMeans(curve_hi),  lwd=2.2, col=col_red)
  legend("topleft", bty="n", legend=c("Low education","Medium education","High education"),
         col=c(col_blue,col_green,col_red), lwd=2.2)
}, w=9, h=4.5)

# ── fig11_int_forest (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig11_int_forest", {
  postI_full <- fit_int$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  gamma_j_mean <- sapply(1:15, function(j) mean(postI_full[,paste0("gamma_sex[",j,"]")]))
  gamma_j_lo   <- sapply(1:15, function(j) quantile(postI_full[,paste0("gamma_sex[",j,"]")],.025))
  gamma_j_hi   <- sapply(1:15, function(j) quantile(postI_full[,paste0("gamma_sex[",j,"]")],.975))
  ages_int <- 16:30
  
  plot(gamma_j_mean, 1:15, xlim=c(-150,250), yaxt="n",
       pch=16, col=col_purp, xlab="gamma_j (words)", ylab="",
       main="Age-Specific Sex Effects (NB_int) vs Pooled Effect (NB3)")
  axis(2, at=1:15, labels=ages_int, las=1, cex.axis=0.8)
  mtext("Age (months)", side=2, line=2.5, cex=0.85)
  segments(gamma_j_lo, 1:15, gamma_j_hi, 1:15, col=col_purp, lwd=1.8)
  abline(v=0, col="gray40", lty=2)
  
  # Overlay NB3 pooled gamma as a shaded vertical band
  gamma3_ci <- quantile(fit_nb3$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix[,"gamma"], c(.025,.975))
  rect(gamma3_ci[1], -1, gamma3_ci[2], 17, col=adjustcolor(col_green,0.15), border=NA)
  abline(v=mean(fit_nb3$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix[,"gamma"]), col=col_green, lwd=1.5)
  legend("topright", bty="n", cex=0.78,
         legend=c("NB_int: gamma_j (age-specific)","NB3: pooled gamma (95% CI band)"),
         col=c(col_purp,col_green), lwd=c(1.8,8), pt.cex=0)
}, w=9, h=5)

# ── fig12_param_recovery (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig12_param_recovery", {
  post_sim  <- fit_sim$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  true_vals <- c(mu_alpha=450, beta=0.06, sigma_alpha=150, r=1.6)
  
  par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar=c(4,4,3,1))
  for (param in names(true_vals)) {
    s    <- post_sim[, param]
    ci95 <- quantile(s, c(0.025, 0.975))
    in_ci <- true_vals[param] >= ci95[1] & true_vals[param] <= ci95[2]
    plot(density(s), main=paste0(param, " [", ifelse(in_ci,"OK","FAIL"), "]"),
         xlab=param, col=col_purp, lwd=2)
    polygon(density(s), col=adjustcolor(col_purp,.15), border=NA)
    abline(v=true_vals[param], col=col_red,   lwd=2.5, lty=2)
    abline(v=mean(s),          col=col_green, lwd=2,   lty=3)
    legend("topright",
           c(paste("True =",true_vals[param]),
             paste("Post.mean =",round(mean(s),3))),
           col=c(col_red,col_green), lwd=2, cex=0.8)
  }
  par(mfrow=c(1,1))
}, w=9, h=6)

# ── fig15_bayes_mle (base-R) ──

# ── fig16_shrinkage_n (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig16_shrinkage_n", {

  n_match   <- as.numeric(n_per_age[match(comparison$age, names(n_per_age))])
  n_match[is.na(n_match)] <- 0
  
  plot(n_match, comparison$shrinkage, pch=16, col=col_purp, cex=1.3,
       xlab="Number of children at this age (n)", ylab="Shrinkage (Bayes - MLE, words)",

}, w=9, h=4)

# ── fig17_dic_comparison (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig17_dic_comparison", {
  dic_vals  <- dic_table$DIC
  names(dic_vals) <- dic_table$Model
  
  # Two-panel DIC plot: left shows the full scale including P0,
  # right zooms into the NegBin models only for readability
  par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(5,4,3,1))
  
  # LEFT: full scale
  bar_cols_full <- c("#8B0000", col_red, col_green, col_green,
                     col_green, "#CC8800", "#CC8800")
  bp_full <- barplot(dic_vals, col=adjustcolor(bar_cols_full,0.80),
                     border=bar_cols_full, ylab="DIC",
                     names.arg=dic_table$Model, cex.names=0.78,
                     main="All models (full scale)")
  abline(h=dic_vals[3], col=col_green, lty=2, lwd=1.5)
  
  # RIGHT: NegBin models only (zoomed)
  nb_vals  <- dic_vals[2:7]
  nb_names <- names(dic_vals)[2:7]
  nb_cols  <- bar_cols_full[2:7]
  y_lo <- min(nb_vals) - 15
  y_hi <- max(nb_vals) + 15
  bp_nb <- barplot(nb_vals, col=adjustcolor(nb_cols,0.80),
                   border=nb_cols, ylim=c(y_lo, y_hi), xpd=FALSE,
                   ylab="DIC", names.arg=nb_names, cex.names=0.78,
                   main="NegBin models only (zoomed)")
  abline(h=dic_vals[3], col=col_green, lty=2, lwd=1.5)
  text(bp_nb, nb_vals + 3, sprintf("%.1f", nb_vals), cex=0.72, xpd=NA)
  par(mfrow=c(1,1))
}, w=9, h=5)

# ── fig18_alpha_comparison (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig18_alpha_comparison", {
  post3_cmp <- fit_nb3$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  post6_cmp <- fit_nb6$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  age_grid3 <- 16:30
  
  alpha_nb2 <- sapply(1:15, function(j) mean(post2_full[, paste0("alpha[",j,"]")]))
  
  m_nb3 <- sapply(1:15, function(j) mean(post3_cmp[, paste0("alpha[",j,"]")]))
  g_nb3 <- mean(post3_cmp[,"gamma"])
  b_nb3 <- mean(post3_cmp[,"beta"])
  male_nb3   <- m_nb3 * (1 - exp(-b_nb3*(age_grid3-8)))
  female_nb3 <- (m_nb3 + g_nb3) * (1 - exp(-b_nb3*(age_grid3-8)))
  
  mu_alpha_nb6 <- mean(post6_cmp[,"mu_alpha"])
  b1_nb6 <- mean(post6_cmp[,"beta[1]"]); b2_nb6 <- mean(post6_cmp[,"beta[2]"])
  male_nb6   <- mu_alpha_nb6 * (1 - exp(-b1_nb6*(age_grid3-8)))
  female_nb6 <- mu_alpha_nb6 * (1 - exp(-b2_nb6*(age_grid3-8)))
  
  plot(age_grid3, alpha_nb2*(1-exp(-mean(post2_full[,"beta"])*(age_grid3-8))),
       type="l", lwd=2, col="gray40", lty=2,
       ylim=c(0,650), xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Predicted vocabulary",
       main="Model Comparison: NB2 vs Sex-Specific Curves (NB3, NB6)")
  lines(age_grid3, male_nb3,   col=col_blue, lwd=2.2, lty=1)
  lines(age_grid3, female_nb3, col=col_red,  lwd=2.2, lty=1)
  lines(age_grid3, male_nb6,   col=col_blue, lwd=2.2, lty=3)
  lines(age_grid3, female_nb6, col=col_red,  lwd=2.2, lty=3)
  legend("topleft", bty="n", cex=0.78,
         legend=c("NB2 (no sex)","NB3 male","NB3 female","NB6 male","NB6 female"),
         col=c("gray40",col_blue,col_red,col_blue,col_red), lwd=2, lty=c(2,1,1,3,3))
}, w=9, h=5)

# ── fig19_predictive_snapshot (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig19_predictive_snapshot", {
  post3 <- fit_nb3$BUGSoutput$sims.matrix
  ages_pred <- c(18, 24, 30)
  
  par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  
  for (eta in ages_pred) {
    j     <- eta - 15
    a_idx <- paste0("alpha[", j, "]")
    n_pred <- 5000
    idx_s  <- sample(nrow(post3), n_pred, replace = TRUE)
  
    mu_male   <- post3[idx_s, a_idx] *
                 (1 - exp(-post3[idx_s, "beta"] * (eta - 8)))
    mu_female <- (post3[idx_s, a_idx] + post3[idx_s, "gamma"]) *
                 (1 - exp(-post3[idx_s, "beta"] * (eta - 8)))
  
    y_pred_male   <- pmin(rnbinom(n_pred, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_male),   680)
    y_pred_female <- pmin(rnbinom(n_pred, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_female), 680)
  
    d_m <- density(y_pred_male,   from=0, to=700)
    d_f <- density(y_pred_female, from=0, to=700)
  
    plot(d_m, col=col_blue, lwd=2.5,
         xlim=c(0, 720), ylim=c(0, max(d_m$y, d_f$y)*1.15),
         main=paste0("Age: ", eta, " months"),
         xlab="Productive vocabulary", ylab="Density")
    polygon(d_m, col=adjustcolor(col_blue, 0.12), border=NA)
    lines(d_f, col=col_red, lwd=2.5)
    polygon(d_f, col=adjustcolor(col_red, 0.12), border=NA)
    abline(v=680, col="gray50", lty=3, lwd=1.5)
  
    legend("topright", bty="n",
           legend=c(sprintf("Male:   median=%d", round(median(y_pred_male))),
                    sprintf("Female: median=%d", round(median(y_pred_female)))),
           col=c(col_blue, col_red), lwd=2, cex=0.82)
  }
  par(mfrow=c(1,1))
}, w=9, h=4)

# ── fig20_fan_chart (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig20_fan_chart", {
  ages_fan <- 16:30
  fan_male <- fan_female <- matrix(NA, nrow=length(ages_fan), ncol=5)
  colnames(fan_male) <- colnames(fan_female) <- c("p10","p25","p50","p75","p90")
  
  set.seed(7)
  for (k in seq_along(ages_fan)) {
    eta <- ages_fan[k]; j <- eta-15; a_idx <- paste0("alpha[",j,"]")
    idx_s <- sample(nrow(post3), 4000, replace=TRUE)
    mu_m <- post3[idx_s,a_idx]*(1-exp(-post3[idx_s,"beta"]*(eta-8)))
    mu_f <- (post3[idx_s,a_idx]+post3[idx_s,"gamma"])*(1-exp(-post3[idx_s,"beta"]*(eta-8)))
    ym <- pmin(rnbinom(4000, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_m), 680)
    yf <- pmin(rnbinom(4000, size=post3[idx_s,"r"], mu=mu_f), 680)
    fan_male[k,]   <- quantile(ym, c(.10,.25,.50,.75,.90))
    fan_female[k,] <- quantile(yf, c(.10,.25,.50,.75,.90))
  }
  
  par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4,4,3,1))
  plot(ages_fan, fan_male[,"p50"], type="n", ylim=c(0,690),
       xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Productive vocabulary", main="Boys - predictive fan")
  polygon(c(ages_fan,rev(ages_fan)), c(fan_male[,"p10"],rev(fan_male[,"p90"])),
          col=adjustcolor(col_blue,0.18), border=NA)
  polygon(c(ages_fan,rev(ages_fan)), c(fan_male[,"p25"],rev(fan_male[,"p75"])),
          col=adjustcolor(col_blue,0.35), border=NA)
  lines(ages_fan, fan_male[,"p50"], col=col_blue, lwd=2.5)
  abline(h=680, col=col_red, lty=3)
  
  plot(ages_fan, fan_female[,"p50"], type="n", ylim=c(0,690),
       xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Productive vocabulary", main="Girls - predictive fan")
  polygon(c(ages_fan,rev(ages_fan)), c(fan_female[,"p10"],rev(fan_female[,"p90"])),
          col=adjustcolor(col_red,0.18), border=NA)
  polygon(c(ages_fan,rev(ages_fan)), c(fan_female[,"p25"],rev(fan_female[,"p75"])),
          col=adjustcolor(col_red,0.35), border=NA)
  lines(ages_fan, fan_female[,"p50"], col=col_red, lwd=2.5)
  abline(h=680, col=col_red, lty=3)
  par(mfrow=c(1,1))
}, w=9, h=5)

# ── fig21_executive_summary (base-R) ──
save_fig("fig21_executive_summary", {
  par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar=c(4,4,3,1))
  
  # Panel 1: overdispersion ratio by age
  plot(desc$age, desc$var_mean_ratio, type="b", pch=16, col=col_red, lwd=2,
       xlab="Age (months)", ylab="Var / Mean", main="(A) Overdispersion by age",
       ylim=c(0,160))
  abline(h=1, col="gray50", lty=2, lwd=1.5)
  text(17, 10, "Poisson threshold = 1", cex=0.7, col="gray40", pos=3)
  
  # Panel 2: DIC by model (NegBin models only for readability — P0 would dwarf the others)
  nb_dic_vals  <- dic_vals[2:7]
  nb_dic_names <- dic_table$Model[2:7]
  nb_dic_cols  <- c(col_red, col_green, col_green, col_green, "#CC8800", "#CC8800")
  barplot(pmin(nb_dic_vals, 6440), col=adjustcolor(nb_dic_cols, 0.75), border=nb_dic_cols,
          ylim=c(6390, 6440), xpd=FALSE, ylab="DIC", main="(B) DIC by NegBin model",
          names.arg=nb_dic_names, cex.names=0.7)
  abline(h=dic_table$DIC[3], col=col_green, lty=2)  # NB2 is row 3 (after P0)
  
  # Panel 3: sex gap comparison
  gap_alpha   <- mean(post3_cmp[,"gamma"])
  gap_alpha_ci<- quantile(post3_cmp[,"gamma"], c(.025,.975))
  half_male   <- log(2)/post6_cmp[,"beta[1]"]
  half_female <- log(2)/post6_cmp[,"beta[2]"]
  gap_months  <- mean(half_male - half_female)
  gap_months_ci <- quantile(half_male - half_female, c(.025,.975))
  
  bp2 <- barplot(c(gap_alpha, NA), ylim=c(0,120), col=col_green,
                 names.arg=c("Sex gap on\nvocabulary level\n(words, NB3)",""),
                 main="(C) Sex effects: level vs timing", ylab="Effect size")
  arrows(bp2[1], gap_alpha_ci[1], bp2[1], gap_alpha_ci[2], angle=90, code=3, length=0.05)
  par(new=TRUE)
  bp3 <- barplot(c(NA, gap_months), ylim=c(0,6), col=col_purp, axes=FALSE,
                 names.arg=c("","Sex gap on\ntiming\n(months, NB6)"), ylab="")
  axis(4)
  mtext("Months earlier (girls)", side=4, line=2.2, cex=0.7)
  arrows(bp3[2], gap_months_ci[1], bp3[2], gap_months_ci[2], angle=90, code=3, length=0.05)
  
  # Panel 4: predictive band at 24 months
  j24 <- 24-15; a_idx24 <- paste0("alpha[",j24,"]")
  idx24 <- sample(nrow(post3), 4000, replace=TRUE)
  mu_m24 <- post3[idx24,a_idx24]*(1-exp(-post3[idx24,"beta"]*(24-8)))
  mu_f24 <- (post3[idx24,a_idx24]+post3[idx24,"gamma"])*(1-exp(-post3[idx24,"beta"]*(24-8)))
  ym24 <- pmin(rnbinom(4000,size=post3[idx24,"r"],mu=mu_m24),680)
  yf24 <- pmin(rnbinom(4000,size=post3[idx24,"r"],mu=mu_f24),680)
  
  boxplot(list(Boys=ym24, Girls=yf24), col=c(adjustcolor(col_blue,0.5),adjustcolor(col_red,0.5)),
          main="(D) Predictive distribution at 24mo", ylab="Productive vocabulary")
  
  par(mfrow=c(1,1))
}, w=9, h=7)
